claims.text: PtPdCoCuNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can be synthesized by a one-pot solvothermal method.
The relevant solvothermal synthesis uses an inert atmosphere, controlled precursor concentrations, and a 150–300 °C reaction-temperature window.
Rapid cooling minimizes elemental segregation in noble-metal-based HEA nanoparticles.
Reduced elemental segregation produces a more uniform distribution of catalytically active sites.
A more uniform distribution of active sites enhances catalytic performance.
Elemental dispersion and HEA phase uniformity determine the distribution of catalytically active sites.
Rapid cooling limits atomic diffusion during nucleation.
Limiting atomic diffusion suppresses elemental segregation.
Homogeneous dispersion of noble-metal active sites supports favorable electronic interactions among the constituent metals.
Electronic interactions and charge transfer among the metals modify adsorption on Pt/Pd sites and enhance nitrobenzene hydrogenation performance.
Slow cooling permits more elemental segregation than rapid quenching.
Greater segregation causes heterogeneous active-site distributions that are suboptimal for catalysis.
Rapidly quenched PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles will have a more uniform elemental distribution than otherwise identical slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will contain a higher density of optimally configured active sites than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit higher turnover frequencies and selectivity for reactions such as nitrobenzene hydrogenation than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Formation of the PtPdCoCuNi HEA creates highly isolated, nucleophilic Pt and Pd active sites.
PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 exhibits high activity for selective nitrobenzene hydrogenation.
The proposed cooling-rate effect should hold for similar noble-metal-based HEAs synthesized under inert atmosphere at 150–300 °C.
Substantially different alloy systems or synthesis conditions may show a different relationship between cooling rate, segregation, and catalytic behavior.
Controlled experiments on PtPdCoCuNi systems already support the proposed rapid-quench versus slow-cooling hypothesis.
